subject: react
title: State and Interactive Forms
summary: Predict state updates, build controlled forms and choose reliable state ownership, identity and reducer rules.

lessons.title: State is a render snapshot
lessons.summary: Predict what a handler reads before and after requesting a state update.
lessons.body:
A state setter requests a future render; it does not rewrite the state variable in the function already running. Each render receives a **state snapshot**. The JSX and event handlers created by that render use that snapshot.

This distinction answers a common beginner question: “Why did I read the old number immediately after setting it?” You read the number that belongs to the current render. React will call the component again with the next value and create new handlers for that render.

## Trace a single click

The following component function assumes `useState` is imported from React and JSX is transformed by a React-enabled build. Its `report` prop is a function supplied by the parent; it records the value passed to it. It is a teaching example inside an event handler, not logging during render.

```jsx
function Counter({ report }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    report(count);
  }
  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick}>
      {count}
    </button>
  );
}
```

Initially the button displays 0. The first click requests 1, then reports 0. After React processes the update, the button displays 1. A second click uses the new handler: it requests 2 and reports 1. Calling the setter is not an instruction to change the existing `count` binding halfway through the handler.

A normal local variable also does not remember values between component calls. React state supplies that memory. Directly assigning to a local variable will not tell React to display a new result.

## Delayed work keeps its captured values

A JavaScript **closure** lets a function retain access to the variables from where it was created. A delayed callback created by a handler therefore keeps that render's state values. It does not automatically switch to values from a later render.

For example, suppose a Send handler schedules a message using the currently selected recipient. Changing the selection before the callback runs does not change the already captured recipient. Decide whether the operation should use the value at the time of the click or a later value; do not assume those are interchangeable. We will use functional updates next when an update needs the latest pending state.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A printed order slip
> A waiter prints the order as it stood when you pressed Send. Later edits make a new order slip.
>
> **How it maps:** The printed slip is a render snapshot; its handler reads those recorded values even after requesting another render.
>
> **Where it stops:** React state is held by React, and JavaScript closures capture bindings. There is no literal copy of every object: mutating shared objects can corrupt older snapshots.

## Key takeaways
- A handler reads the state snapshot of the render that created it.
- Setters request another render; they do not change the current state binding.
- Delayed callbacks retain their captured values unless you deliberately design another mechanism.

## Further reading
- [State as a snapshot](https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot)
- [useState reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useState)
- [Closures — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Closures)

lessons.title: Queue state updates deliberately
lessons.summary: Choose replacement or functional updates and trace their order.
lessons.body:
Sometimes one event needs several changes to the same state. React processes queued updates to calculate the next value. **Batching** groups updates so React can display the resulting state together after the event handler finishes. Do not expect the screen to update between two setter calls in that handler.

## A value requests a replacement

Here is a handler excerpt inside a component whose `count` state is initially 0. Both lines evaluate their argument using the same snapshot.

```js
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);
```

Both requests mean “replace with 1”, so the next displayed count is 1, not 2. The second line does not read the result of the first request.

## A function transforms the pending value

An **updater function** receives the pending value from React's update queue. This handler excerpt uses arrow functions: `n => n + 1` means “take a value named n and return one more”.

```js
setCount(n => n + 1);
setCount(n => n + 1);
```

Starting at 0, the first updater returns 1. React passes that pending result to the second updater, which returns 2. This expresses two increments without depending on the handler's older snapshot. Prefer this form when the next state depends on the previous state.

Replacement and functional updates can be mixed. Starting at 0, trace this excerpt from top to bottom:

```js
setCount(5);
setCount(n => n + 1);
setCount(2);
```

The replacement chooses 5. The updater transforms that to 6. The final replacement chooses 2, so the next count is 2. This is an ordered queue, not a rule that all increments must win.

## Keep updaters pure

A **pure updater** calculates and returns the next state without modifying old state or doing external work. Do not send requests, change another state variable, or write to external arrays inside an updater. Put event-specific external work in the handler instead. In development Strict Mode, React may call updater functions twice to expose accidental impurities; one result is ignored. Correct logic must not depend on the number of updater calls.

React does not batch separate intentional clicks into one event. For this lesson, trace each handler in order, then consider the next interaction with the newly displayed state. Batching is useful behaviour, not a timer you should attempt to exploit for correctness.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Editing instructions in order
> A clerk receives “use 5”, “add one”, then “use 2” before updating a display.
>
> **How it maps:** Replacement updates choose a pending value; updater functions transform the current pending value in queue order.
>
> **Where it stops:** The clerk is only a model of this queue. React can perform additional internal work, and pure updater functions must tolerate repeated development checks.

## Key takeaways
- Repeating a snapshot-based replacement does not accumulate increments.
- Functional updates receive the pending value and compose in order.
- Updaters must only calculate state; keep external work outside them.

## Further reading
- [Queueing state updates](https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates)
- [useState caveats](https://react.dev/reference/react/useState)

lessons.title: Update objects without mutation
lessons.summary: Copy changed object paths and preserve previous state snapshots.

questions.prompt: A profile has name “Mina” and address `{ city: "Leeds", postcode: "A1" }`. You change only its city to York. Which objects need copying for a direct immutable update?

options.text: Only the address, while editing profile.address in place
options.explanation: Assigning the new address into the existing profile would mutate state.

options.text: Only the profile, then edit its shared address
options.explanation: A shallow outer copy still refers to the same nested address.

options.text: Both the profile and its address
options.explanation: Copy each object on the changed path, then preserve the untouched fields.

options.text: Every object in the application
options.explanation: Unrelated branches can be reused when they remain read-only.

questions.workedExample:
1. The city is inside address, so create a new address with the old postcode and new city.
2. Address is inside profile, so create a new profile pointing to that new address.
3. Preserve the name.
4. The old profile and old address still describe Leeds.

options.text: Object spread changes every nested object
options.explanation: Spread copies the outer level, not all nested objects.

options.text: It mutates the address before copying
options.explanation: The first line edits an object still reachable through the old state.

options.text: The setter cannot accept an object
options.explanation: Object state can be replaced with a new object.

options.text: York is an invalid state value
options.explanation: The problem is the mutation mechanism, not this string.

questions.workedExample:
1. The assignment changes the existing address.
2. Every reference to that address can now observe York.
3. The outer spread creates a new profile but shares the mutated address.
4. Copy the address before changing city instead.

questions.prompt: A functional object update returns `{ ...previous, city: "York" }`. Select all true statements.

options.text: The returned outer object is new
options.explanation: Object spread is used inside a new object literal.

options.text: Every nested object has also been copied
options.explanation: Spread is shallow; unchanged nested values can still refer to existing objects.

options.text: The existing city field is replaced by York
options.explanation: The property written after the spread wins over that earlier property.

options.text: Returning a new object requires mutating previous first
options.explanation: The purpose is to construct the replacement without editing previous.

questions.workedExample:
1. A new object literal receives the previous own enumerable properties.
2. The later city property overrides the earlier city value.
3. Other fields remain available.
4. Nested references are shared unless explicitly copied, so they must remain read-only.

questions.prompt: You need to remove task 7 and sort the remaining tasks. Select all safe choices when callbacks only read items.

options.text: Use filter to keep items whose id is not 7
options.explanation: filter returns a new array without editing the original.

options.text: Call sort directly on the state array
options.explanation: sort rearranges its receiver in place, mutating state.

options.text: Copy the state array, then sort the copy
options.explanation: Sorting a new array preserves the order of the original array.

options.text: Use splice directly on the state array
options.explanation: splice mutates its receiver; it is not an immutable removal.

questions.workedExample:
1. Remove by calculating a filtered array.
2. If sorting an existing state array, first create a separate array with spread.
3. Sort only that fresh array.
4. Keep comparison and filter callbacks free from item mutation.

lessons.title: Control inputs with state
lessons.summary: Connect labelled text and checkbox inputs to state and handle submission.
lessons.body:
A **controlled input** displays a value supplied by React state. User edits call an event handler, which immediately updates that state. React then renders the accepted value. For text, connect `value` to a string and read `event.target.value`. For a checkbox, connect `checked` to a boolean and read `event.target.checked`.

An **uncontrolled input** instead keeps its current value in the browser; `defaultValue` or `defaultChecked` supplies only its initial value. Both approaches have uses. This lesson uses controlled inputs so the application can calculate what to display from state.

## A small complete component

This component function assumes `useState` is imported and JSX is transformed. The parent supplies an `onSave` callback; it receives a plain object. Wrapping each input in a visible `label` associates the control with its name.

```jsx
function TaskForm({ onSave }) {
  const [title, setTitle] = useState('');
  const [done, setDone] = useState(false);
  function handleSubmit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    onSave({ title, done });
  }
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <label>
        Task
        <input value={title}
          onChange={event =>
            setTitle(event.target.value)} />
      </label>
      <label>
        <input type="checkbox"
          checked={done}
          onChange={event =>
            setDone(event.target.checked)}
        />
        Complete
      </label>
      <button type="submit">
        Save
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

Typing “Read” updates `title` through the text change handler. Clicking Complete updates `done` through the checkbox handler. Submitting then passes `{ title: 'Read', done: true }` to `onSave`. This example saves through a callback; it does not make a network request or guarantee persistence after a reload.

## Submission and input pitfalls

The form's `onSubmit` handles submission, including keyboard submission where supported by the browser. `preventDefault` stops the form's normal navigation; it does not automatically stop event propagation. A submit button is explicit here. Give any other button inside the form `type="button"` if it should perform a local action without submitting.

A controlled text input needs a string throughout its lifetime. Initialise it to an empty string instead of `undefined` or `null`; otherwise it can switch between uncontrolled and controlled behaviour. Its change handler must synchronously update the state used by `value`. Passing a fixed `value` without such an update makes the field effectively read-only. A checkbox uses `checked`, not its `value` string, for the selected state.

For a separate label, JSX uses `htmlFor` to match an input's unique `id`. A placeholder is not a replacement for a visible label. The association helps users understand and activate the control.

## Key takeaways
- Control text with value/string and checkboxes with checked/boolean.
- Update the controlling state immediately in onChange.
- Use visible labels and handle form submission deliberately.

## Further reading
- [Input reference](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/input)
- [preventDefault — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/preventDefault)

questions.prompt: A form should save through a callback without normal page navigation. It also has a local Clear button. Which design fits?

options.text: Handle only the Save button’s click and make both buttons submit
options.explanation: The Clear button would also submit, and form-level handling better represents submission.

options.text: Call stopPropagation and assume navigation is cancelled
options.explanation: Stopping propagation is separate from cancelling the default form action.

options.text: Use onSubmit with preventDefault, and give Clear type="button"
options.explanation: The form handles submission while the local action avoids submitting.

options.text: Remove the form element because React cannot handle it
options.explanation: React supports forms and their submit events.

questions.workedExample:
1. Put save behaviour in the form’s onSubmit handler.
2. Call preventDefault there to cancel usual browser navigation.
3. Invoke the save callback with current state.
4. Mark Clear as a non-submit button so its local action does not trigger saving.

lessons.title: Give shared state one owner
lessons.summary: Coordinate sibling controls through a common parent and callback props.

questions.prompt: Two sibling text editors must always display the same value. Where should their shared text usually live?

options.text: In their closest useful common parent
options.explanation: One owner can pass the same current value and update callback to both.

options.text: In a separate local state variable in each sibling
options.explanation: Separate useState calls create independent values that can drift.

options.text: In whichever input was clicked most recently, with no parent value
options.explanation: The other sibling then has no shared source for its displayed value.

options.text: In a prop that each child directly assigns to
options.explanation: Props are read-only; children request changes through callbacks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both editors need the same remembered value.
2. Move that value to their common parent.
3. Pass it to both editors and pass callbacks that request updates.
4. A change in either editor updates the owner and reaches both on the next render.

questions.prompt: A child calls `useState(initialName)` using a prop. The parent later passes a different initialName while the same child identity stays mounted. What should you expect?

options.text: The child’s stored state automatically follows every prop change
options.explanation: The initial state argument does not continuously control stored state.

options.text: React throws because props cannot initialise state
options.explanation: A prop can supply an initial value; it simply does not keep that state synchronised.

options.text: The child must remount on every prop change
options.explanation: Ordinary prop changes alone do not require new component identity.

options.text: Its existing local state remains unless explicitly updated or reset
options.explanation: Initialisation happens on mount; design controlled values or reset behaviour deliberately.

questions.workedExample:
1. On mount, the child uses initialName for its initial state.
2. Later, the parent renders with another prop value.
3. The child retains its state because it is the same mounted identity.
4. Use a controlled prop if the parent should remain the owner.

questions.prompt: A parent owns shared text; an Editor receives value and an onChange callback accepting a string. Select all true statements.

options.text: The editor should edit the value prop directly
options.explanation: A prop supplies data; the child requests updates through its callback.

options.text: The callback can pass event.target.value to the parent
options.explanation: That forwards the next string without exposing the event as the component API.

options.text: Both editors can render the parent’s same text value
options.explanation: A single owner naturally keeps the displays consistent.

options.text: The editor must lift unrelated help-panel state too
options.explanation: Independent local behaviour can remain local when no sibling needs it.

questions.workedExample:
1. The parent passes the current text to both children.
2. The child extracts the string in its event handler.
3. Its callback asks the parent to store that string.
4. The next parent render supplies the same updated text to both editors.

lessons.title: Store the minimum useful state
lessons.summary: Derive display values and represent statuses that cannot be active together directly.

questions.prompt: A search screen has task data and a query. The filtered list can be calculated from those values. What is the clearest starting design?

options.text: Store filtered results separately and update them only when typing
options.explanation: Results can become stale when the task data changes.

options.text: Calculate the filtered list during render
options.explanation: The current tasks and query already determine the result, so no extra state is needed.

options.text: Mutate the original tasks to remove hidden items
options.explanation: Filtering the view should not destroy the underlying task data.

options.text: Always fetch again when filtering locally
options.explanation: A local calculation needs no external request when the data is already available.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify the remembered inputs: tasks and query.
2. Apply the filter to those current inputs during render.
3. Render the resulting list and its length.
4. Any change to either input naturally recalculates the view.

questions.prompt: A submission can be idle, submitting, successful or failed, with exactly one active mode. Which representation best prevents contradictory modes?

options.text: Four independent booleans
options.explanation: These allow combinations such as successful and failed at the same time.

options.text: A permanently true isBusy flag
options.explanation: A fixed flag cannot represent the completed modes.

options.text: One status string with one of the four intended values
options.explanation: A single current mode avoids conflicting simultaneous flags.

options.text: One separate stored state for every message shown
options.explanation: Duplicating display details can create more synchronisation problems.

questions.workedExample:
1. List the permitted modes that cannot be active together.
2. Store the current mode in one status value.
3. Derive isBusy by testing for submitting.
4. Store separate information, such as an error message, only when its content must be remembered.

questions.prompt: A task list supports selection, renaming and deletion. Select all choices that reduce duplicate or contradictory state.

options.text: Store a selected task ID and find its current task during render
options.explanation: The selected task then uses the same current object as the list.

options.text: Store a second selected task object and never refresh it
options.explanation: That copy can retain an old title after the main task changes.

options.text: Handle an absent selected ID after deletion
options.explanation: A deleted item needs an explicit no-selection or equivalent state.

options.text: Store visibleCount separately when it is always the filtered list’s length
options.explanation: A separate count adds another value that can disagree with the list.

questions.workedExample:
1. Keep the task records in one place.
2. Remember only the identity of the selected task.
3. Resolve it against current task data each render.
4. If deletion removes that identity, display a deliberate no-selection result.

lessons.title: Understand when state survives
lessons.summary: Use position, component type and keys to preserve or reset local state deliberately.

questions.prompt: Editable rows should retain the right local state after reordering. Select all appropriate choices.

options.text: Use a stable task ID as the sibling key
options.explanation: The identity follows the task across positions.

lessons.title: Describe state transitions with reducers
lessons.summary: Move related update rules into a pure reducer and trace dispatched actions.

questions.prompt: A counter reducer handles reset by returning `{ ...state, count: 0 }`. Its current state is the plain object `{ count: 4, label: "Score" }`. Which values will be available in the next render’s state?

options.text: The old count and the existing label
options.explanation: The later count property overrides the count copied by the spread.

options.text: Zero, with the label removed
options.explanation: The spread carries forward the label and other unchanged own enumerable fields.

options.text: Zero and the existing label
options.explanation: Reset replaces count while preserving the other fields copied from the previous state.

options.text: No replacement state, because reset changes the previous object in place

questions.prompt: Select all requirements for a reliable reducer.

options.text: Send the save request inside every transition
options.explanation: External requests are side effects and do not belong inside a pure reducer.

options.text: Mutate state and return the same object
options.explanation: This damages previous snapshots and may cause React to skip an update.

options.text: Return new state while preserving fields that must survive
options.explanation: A transition must describe the complete intended next state.

options.text: Produce the same result from the same state and action
options.explanation: Pure transitions tolerate repeated development checks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Read the supplied state and action without editing either.
2. Choose the intended transition from the action type.
3. Return the next state, carrying forward unchanged required fields.
4. Keep requests and event-data creation outside the reducer so repeated evaluation is safe.
